title: Changes we can undo and changes we can't: squashing, bending, heating and cooling

summary.text: Squash a ball of atta dough flat, and you can roll it back into a ball. Cook it on a hot tawa, and it can never be dough again. Your child squashes, bends, twists, cools and heats things from the kitchen, and sorts what happens into two kinds. A reversible change can be undone, like bending a ruler or freezing dough. An irreversible change cannot be undone, like snapping a toothpick or cooking a roti. Heating often makes a change that cannot be undone.
summary.art: A steel plate with three pieces of atta dough: one squashed flat with a palm print, one stiff and frosty from the freezer, and one cooked into a small brown-spotted roti.

intro.hook: Crumple a sheet of paper into a tight ball. Now open it out and press it flat. Is it the same as before?
intro.text: Things around us change shape all the time. We squash them, bend them, twist them, stretch them, heat them and cool them. Some changes can be undone, and the thing goes back to how it was. Some can never be undone. You are going to test which is which, starting with a ball of dough.
intro.art: A child's hands pressing a crumpled sheet of paper flat on a table, with many thin crease lines still showing on it.

outcomes: By the end I can say that squashing, bending, twisting and stretching change the shape of a thing, and it is still made of the same material.
By the end I can sort changes into reversible changes, which can be undone, and irreversible changes, which cannot.
By the end I can show that after a bend, some things spring back, some stay bent and some break.
By the end I can say that cooling can make things stiff or solid, and warming them again often undoes it.
By the end I can say that heating can change some materials for good, like dough into roti or batter into dosa.
By the end I can guess first, give a reason, and then say what my test showed.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of.
terms.example: A tumbler is made of steel. A roti is made of atta. A ruler is made of plastic.
terms.art: A steel tumbler, a roti and a plastic ruler in a row, each with a label.

terms.meaning: To squash something is to press it so it gets flatter or smaller.
terms.example: You squash a ball of dough flat with your palm.
terms.art: A palm pressing down on a ball of dough, making it flat.

terms.meaning: To bend something is to make it curve or fold.
terms.example: You bend a plastic ruler into a curve.
terms.art: Two hands bending a plastic ruler into a gentle curve.

terms.meaning: To twist something is to turn one end one way and the other end the other way.
terms.example: You twist a wet towel to squeeze the water out.
terms.art: Two hands twisting a wet towel, with drops falling.

terms.meaning: To stretch something is to pull it so it gets longer.
terms.example: You stretch a rubber band between two fingers.
terms.art: A rubber band stretched long between a thumb and a finger.

terms.meaning: A reversible change is a change that can be undone, so the thing goes back to how it was.
terms.example: Water freezes into ice in the freezer. The ice melts back into water in the room.
terms.art: An arrow going from water to ice, and another arrow going back from ice to water.

terms.meaning: An irreversible change is a change that cannot be undone.
terms.example: Dosa batter turns into a dosa on a hot tawa. You can never turn the dosa back into batter.
terms.art: An arrow from a bowl of dosa batter to a crisp dosa, with a crossed-out arrow going back.

terms.meaning: A thing springs back when it goes back to its old shape as soon as you let go.
terms.example: A sponge springs back after you squeeze it.
terms.art: A squeezed yellow kitchen sponge, and next to it the same sponge back to its full shape.

explanations.concept: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching change a thing's shape
explanations.context: This card explains what happens when we push or pull on something.
explanations.definition: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching are ways of changing the shape of a thing by pushing or pulling on it. The material it is made of stays the same.
explanations.description: In the dough test, you squashed a ball of dough into a flat disc. Then you rolled it into a long snake, and back into a ball. It changed shape three times. It was still atta dough the whole time. Nothing was added and nothing was taken away. Only its shape changed.
examples: A ball of dough squashed into a flat disc
A plastic ruler bent into a curve
A wet towel twisted to squeeze out water
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a palm squashing dough, hands bending a ruler, hands twisting a towel and fingers stretching a rubber band.

explanations.concept: Reversible changes: changes we can undo
explanations.context: This card explains changes that can be undone.
explanations.definition: A reversible change is a change that can be undone, so the material goes back to how it was before.
explanations.description: In the Dough Test, the squashed dough rolled back into a ball. The dough from the freezer was stiff and cold, but in warm hands it went soft again. In the Bend Test, a plastic ruler bent into a curve and sprang back straight. Melting and freezing are reversible too. Ice melts into water, and water freezes back into ice.
examples: Squashed dough rolled back into a ball
Stiff frozen dough warmed until it is soft again
A bent ruler springing back straight
Ice melting into water, then freezing again
explanations.art: A ball of dough, an arrow to a flat disc, and an arrow back to a ball.

explanations.concept: Irreversible changes: changes we cannot undo
explanations.context: This card explains changes that cannot be undone.
explanations.definition: An irreversible change is a change that cannot be undone. Often, heating makes a new material that cannot turn back into the old one.
explanations.description: In the Dough Test, the soft dough became a stiff roti with brown spots on the hot tawa. When it cooled, you could not roll it into a ball. Soaking it in water only made it soggy. The heat had changed the dough into a new material. A snapped toothpick is irreversible in a different way. It is still wood, but you cannot join it into one piece.
examples: Dosa batter cooked into a dosa
A raw egg cooked until it is hard
explanations.art: A soft dough ball, an arrow to a cooked roti, and a crossed-out arrow going back.

explanations.concept: Why some things spring back and others stay bent
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the bend test.
explanations.definition: A thing springs back when the tiny particles it is made of are pushed a little out of place and then pull back. It stays bent when they are pushed so far that they slide into new places.
explanations.description: Everything is made of tiny particles, far too small to see, that hold on to each other. Bend a ruler a little, and the particles are pushed a little apart. When you let go, they pull back, so the ruler springs straight. Bend a paper clip a lot, and its particles slide into new places and stay there. So the clip stays bent.
examples: A ruler bent a little springs back.
A paper clip bent a lot stays bent.
A strip of foil stays bent even after a small bend.
A toothpick snaps when bent too far.
explanations.art: A zoom-in drawing: rows of tiny round particles in a ruler pushed slightly apart, and in a paper clip slid into a new pattern.

explanations.concept: Can every change be undone, if we find the right way?
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still think about.
explanations.description: Nobody has ever turned a roti back into dough. But scientists have undone some changes people thought were for ever. In 2015, scientists in the USA and Australia used a fast-spinning machine to undo part of the change in a boiled egg white. They could not make a raw egg again. But one tiny part of the cooked egg white went back to how it was when raw.
examples: Cooked egg white partly undone in a laboratory in 2015
Old glass bottles melted down and made into new bottles
A roti, which nobody can turn back into dough

perspectives.explanation: The rules for the tiniest particles work the same forwards and backwards. So a change could be undone in theory. In real life, there are far too many particles to put all of them back.
Some changes are for ever. A cooked dosa or a fired clay pot cannot go back, so you get the shape right before the heat.

explanations.art: A boiled egg cut in half on one side, and on the other side a small spinning glass tube in a laboratory.

agreed.text: Squashing, bending, twisting and stretching change the shape of a thing, but not what it is made of.
agreed.evidence: In the dough test, the dough was squashed, rolled into a snake and rolled into a ball. It was atta dough every time.

agreed.text: Some bends spring back, some stay and some break, depending on the material and on how far you bend it.
agreed.evidence: In the bend test, the ruler sprang back, the foil stayed bent and the toothpick snapped. The same paper clip sprang back from a small bend and stayed bent after a big one.

agreed.text: Cooling makes many materials stiffer or solid, and warming them again often undoes the change.
agreed.evidence: In the Dough Test, the dough from the freezer was stiff and cold. A few minutes in warm hands made it soft enough to roll again.

agreed.text: Heating can change some materials into new materials that cannot be changed back.
agreed.evidence: Cooked dough, cooked dosa batter and a cooked egg never turn back, however much you cool, squash or soak them.

challenging.claim: A cooked egg can never be uncooked, even a little.
challenging.who: Scientists led by Gregory Weiss in California, USA, and Colin Raston in Adelaide, Australia, in 2015.
challenging.for: They spun a liquid made from boiled egg white very fast in a thin glass tube. One kind of tiny part in the egg white unfolded back to its raw shape.
challenging.against: They did not make a whole raw egg again. The egg white needed special chemicals and a machine. In a kitchen, a cooked egg still stays cooked.
challenging.context: This card is about scientists who undid a little of a change everyone thought was for ever.

challenging.claim: Melting can be undone, so plastic can be melted and made into new things again and again for ever.
challenging.who: Many people believe this about recycling.
challenging.for: Many plastics do melt when heated and set hard when they cool, so they can be reshaped.
challenging.against: Each time most plastics are melted, their long, chain-like particles break a little. After a few times, the plastic is too weak to use. Some plastics do not melt at all, and burn instead.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about recycling plastic.

big_questions.q: In the Dough Test, you squashed the dough and rolled it back into a ball. Was it exactly the same ball as before?
big_questions.hint: Could anyone tell, just by looking, what you had done to it?

big_questions.q: Why does heat change dough for good, when squashing it does not?
big_questions.hint: Squashing only moves the dough around. What might heat do inside it?

big_questions.q: A crumpled paper pressed flat still has lines on it. Is that change undone or not?
big_questions.hint: Is the paper flat again? Are the lines gone?

big_questions.q: You grow taller every year, and never shorter again. Is growing up a change that can be undone?
big_questions.hint: Think of a baby photo of yourself. Could you go back to that size?

big_questions.q: If a change cannot be undone, is that always bad?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dosa, a clay pot and a seed growing into a plant.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, many people in Europe thought that heating water could turn some of it into earth. They saw it with their own eyes. When they boiled water in a glass pot for a long time, a fine white powder appeared at the bottom. So they said water slowly changes into earth. In 1768, Antoine Lavoisier, a young chemist in Paris, decided to test it. He weighed an empty glass pot, poured in very clean water and sealed it shut, so nothing could get in or out. Then he kept the water hot for 101 days. The steam rose, cooled on the glass and ran back down as water, again and again. At the end, there was powder, just as people said. But Lavoisier weighed the pot again. It had become lighter, by about as much as the powder weighed. The powder had come from the glass, not from the water. Heating had only turned water into steam and back. The water had not changed into anything new.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That heating water for a long time turns some of it into earth. Lavoisier weighed the sealed pot and showed the powder came from the glass itself.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in 1700s clothes beside a big round glass pot of water warming over a small fire, with a weighing balance on the table.

story.title: Selvi's Pot
story.note: Selvi, Chitra Athai and Karthik are made up. Athai is a Tamil word for a father's sister. It is true that soft or dried clay can be wetted and shaped again, and that clay fired in a hot kiln becomes pottery, which can never turn back into clay.
text: Selvi was seven, and she lived in Chennai. In the summer holidays, she went to stay with Chitra Athai, her father's sister. Athai lived in a village near Madurai, and she was a potter. She made pots, lamps and water jars out of clay.
Selvi's cousin Karthik was six. He had been there for a week already, and he thought he knew everything.
Behind the house there was a heap of grey, wet clay under a sack. Athai pulled off a lump and gave it to Selvi. It was cool and heavy, and it felt like very thick dough.
"Make anything you like," said Athai.

Selvi pressed her thumbs into the lump. She pinched and squeezed the sides. Slowly, a little pot came up between her fingers. But one side was thick and the other side was thin, and the whole pot leaned over like a tired dog.
"It's crooked," said Karthik.
Selvi's face went hot. She wanted to throw the pot on the ground.
Athai picked up the crooked pot. Then she squashed it flat between her palms. She rolled it into a ball, and gave the ball back to Selvi.
"Clay always lets you try again," she said. "Squash it, roll it, start over. It is still clay."
So Selvi tried again. This time her pot came out round, with walls as thick as her finger all the way round. She set it on a plank in the shade to dry.
Two days later, the pot was pale and hard. Karthik tapped it. "It's done," he said. "Now it's a real pot."

"Not yet," said Athai. "Watch." She broke a small piece off the edge of an old dried pot she had thrown away. She dropped it into a tumbler of water. In a few minutes, the piece went soft. Athai squeezed it, and it was sticky clay again.
Selvi stared. "Drying can be undone?"
"Drying can be undone," said Athai. "Water dried out of the clay. Put the water back, and it is clay again. A dried pot is still clay. If it rains on it, it turns to mud."
"So how do you make a real pot?" asked Selvi.

Athai pointed to a round mud oven at the end of the yard. It was taller than Selvi. "That is my kiln," she said. "It gets much hotter than any kitchen. Hotter than a tawa, hotter than a cooker. We will fire your pot in it."

The next day, Athai filled the kiln with pots, lamps and Selvi's little pot. She lit the fire, and she kept it burning all day and late into the night. The yard smelled of smoke. Nobody was allowed to go near.

In the morning, when the kiln had cooled, Athai lifted the pots out. Selvi's pot was not grey any more. It was a warm orange-red, the colour of a flowerpot. When Selvi tapped it with her nail, it made a little ringing sound, like a bell.
"Now drop a piece of that in water," said Athai. She gave Selvi a chip from a broken red pot.
Selvi dropped it into the tumbler. She waited. She counted to a hundred. She squeezed the chip. It was still hard.
Karthik squeezed it too. He even left it in the water all through lunch. It stayed hard and red.
"The fire changed it," said Athai. "Clay that has been fired becomes a new material. We call it pottery. It will never be clay again. Not with water, not with squashing, not with anything."
Selvi looked at her red pot. She ran her finger round the rim. She saw her own fingerprint pressed into the side, from the day she made it. It would be there for ever now.
"So that is why you let me squash the crooked one," she said slowly. "Before the fire, you can always try again. After the fire, it stays."
Athai smiled. "That is the first thing every potter learns," she said. "Get the shape right while the clay is soft."
That evening, Selvi taught Karthik how to make a pot with walls as thick as his finger all the way round. His leaned over too. Selvi squashed it into a ball and gave it back to him.
"Clay always lets you try again," she said.
story.epiphany: Squashing and drying clay can be undone, but the great heat of the kiln changes clay into pottery for ever.
ask: What could Selvi do to her crooked pot before the fire? Why?
Why did the dried piece go soft in water, but the fired piece stay hard?
Selvi's fingerprint stayed in her pot for ever. What else around you keeps a mark of how it was made?

A woman potter dropping a small grey chip of dried clay into a steel tumbler of water.
A round mud kiln at the end of a yard, with smoke rising from it at dusk.

experiments.title: The Dough Test: squash it, freeze it, cook it. Can it go back?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make three equal pieces of atta dough. You squash one, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooks one on a hot tawa. Then you try to make each one a soft ball again.
experiments.question: We can change dough by squashing it, by cooling it and by heating it. Which of these changes can we undo?
experiments.predict: Look at the three pieces of dough. After we squash one, freeze one and cook one, which ones can you roll back into a soft ball? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three pieces come from the same ball of dough, and they are the same size. We try to undo each change in the same way, by rolling it in our hands. We check every piece only after it has warmed up or cooled down to the warmth of the room.
results_table: My guess: can it go back?
What it looked and felt like
Did it become a soft ball again?

materials.item: half a cup of atta, or ragi flour or rice flour, and a little water, to make a soft dough the size of a lemon
a steel plate
a small piece of cling film, or a small steel box, for the freezer piece
space in the freezer (the fridge works too, but more slowly)
a tawa or a flat pan, and the stove, used only by a grown-up
a rolling pin, or a steel tumbler to press with
a small bowl of water
a pencil and paper for the results table

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the stove and the hot tawa. Let the cooked piece cool for 2 minutes on the plate before your child touches it.

schedule.what: Make three equal pieces of dough. Squash one, freeze one and cook one. Try to roll each one back into a soft ball.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw each piece after its change, and write 'went back' or 'did not go back' under it.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Squashed flat, rolled into a snake
Flat, then long and thin, still soft
Stiff and very cold, would not bend
Yes, after 4 minutes in warm hands
Stiff, dry, with brown spots. It tore when rolled
No. In water it went soggy, not doughy

setup.art: A lemon-sized ball of atta dough on a steel plate, being cut into three equal pieces with a butter knife.
setup.caption: 1. Make a ball of dough. Cut it into three equal pieces.

setup.art: A child's palm squashing one piece flat, and then rolling it into a long snake.
setup.caption: 2. Squash piece 1 flat. Roll it into a snake. Then roll it into a ball.

setup.art: A flat disc of dough in a small steel box going into the freezer.
setup.caption: 3. Press piece 2 into a flat disc. Put it in the freezer.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand turning a small disc of dough on a hot tawa, with brown spots on it.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up cooks piece 3 on a hot tawa.

setup.art: Three pieces side by side on a plate: a soft ball, a stiff frosty disc and a small cooked roti.
setup.caption: 5. Try to make each piece a soft ball again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the dough test. You make the dough and guess.
flow.do: 1. Make a soft dough the size of a lemon, or use dough left from cooking. 2. Cut it into three equal pieces. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: These three pieces are the same dough. I will squash one, freeze one and cook one. Afterwards, which ones can you roll back into a soft ball? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the three pieces. One gets squashed. One gets frozen. One gets cooked. Which can go back to a soft ball? Why?

ask.q: Which pieces will go back to a soft ball? Why?
good: The squashed one, because I can roll it again.
Not the frozen one, because it will be hard like ice.
Not the cooked one, because a roti is not dough.

flow.parent: Write your child's guess for each piece in the table. Do not say which guess is right. Many children think the frozen piece will stay hard for ever.

flow.context: In this step of the dough test, piece 2 goes into the freezer first, because it needs time.
flow.do: 1. Your child presses piece 2 into a flat disc, about as thick as a coin. 2. Wrap it in cling film or put it in a small box. 3. Put it in the freezer and note the time.
flow.say: Press this piece flat, as thin as a coin. Thin pieces get cold faster. Now it goes into the freezer for 15 minutes.
flow.kid: Press piece 2 flat and thin. Put it in the freezer. Look at the clock.
flow.parent: If you have no freezer, use the fridge for 30 minutes. The dough will get firmer, but not as stiff.

flow.context: In this step of the dough test, you squash piece 1 and try to undo it.
flow.do: 1. Your child squashes piece 1 flat with a palm. 2. Then rolls it into a long snake. 3. Then rolls it back into a ball. 4. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Squash it flat. Now roll it into a long snake. Now can you make it a ball again? Is it still dough?
flow.kid: Squash piece 1 flat. Roll it into a snake. Now roll it into a ball again. Is it still dough?

ask.q: Is it the same dough as before? How do you know?
good: Yes, it is still soft and sticky.
Yes, nothing was added. Only the shape changed.

flow.parent: The dough goes back to a ball every time. Let your child squash and roll it two or three times.

flow.context: In this step of the dough test, a grown-up cooks piece 3 on a hot tawa.
flow.do: 1. Roll piece 3 into a small, thin disc. 2. Heat the tawa. 3. Cook the disc for about one minute on each side. 4. Put it on the plate to cool for 2 minutes.
flow.say: Stand back from the stove and watch. What is happening to the dough on the tawa? What colour is it turning?
flow.kid: Stand back from the stove. Watch the dough on the tawa. What do you see?

ask.q: What is happening to the dough?
good: It is getting brown spots.
It is puffing up a little.
It is getting dry and stiff.

flow.parent: Use a medium flame. The disc stiffens, gets brown spots and may puff. It is now a small roti. Keep your child at arm's length from the stove.

flow.context: In this step of the dough test, you try to undo the cooked piece.
flow.do: 1. When the cooked piece is cool, your child tries to roll it into a soft ball. 2. Tear off a small bit and put it in the bowl of water for 3 minutes. 3. Squeeze the wet bit.
flow.say: Can you roll the cooked piece into a soft ball, like the first one? Let's try water too. Does water turn it back into dough?
flow.kid: Try to roll the cooked piece into a ball. Put a bit in water. Squeeze it. Is it dough again?

ask.q: Did the cooked piece become dough again?
good: No. It tore and would not roll.
No. In water it went soggy, but not sticky like dough.

flow.parent: The roti tears or folds but will not become a smooth, sticky ball. In water it goes soft and soggy, but it does not become dough. Let your child decide that for themselves.

flow.context: In this step of the dough test, you take piece 2 out of the freezer and try to undo it.
flow.do: 1. Take piece 2 out of the freezer. 2. Your child tries to bend it. 3. Then holds it in both hands for 4 minutes. 4. Then tries to roll it into a ball.
flow.say: Feel it. Can you bend it? Now hold it in your warm hands while we count. Is it changing? Can you roll it into a ball now?
flow.kid: Feel the frozen piece. Can you bend it? Hold it in your warm hands. Now roll it into a ball.

ask.q: What happened to the frozen piece in your hands?
good: It was stiff and cold, then it went soft.
It rolled into a ball again.

flow.parent: The water in the dough froze, so the disc went stiff. Warm hands melt it, and in about 3 to 5 minutes the dough is soft again. If it is still hard, wait 2 minutes more.

flow.context: This is the last step of the dough test. You say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Put the three pieces side by side. 2. Ask your child which changes could be undone, what they saw, and why they think so. 3. Then read the cards on reversible and irreversible changes.
flow.say: Look at all three. Which changes could you undo? What did you see that tells you? Why do you think the tawa changed the dough for good?
flow.kid: Look at the three pieces. Which changes could you undo? Which could you not? Why?

ask.q: Why couldn't the cooked piece go back?
good: The heat made it into roti, which is a new material.
The heat changed what was inside it, not only its shape.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses what your child saw: 'The squashed one and the frozen one became soft balls again. The cooked one tore and went soggy.' Only after that, explain that heat can make a new material.

experiments.title: The Bend Test: does it spring back, stay bent or break?
experiments.context: In this experiment you gently bend six things from home: a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a strip of foil, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick. You watch what each one does when you let go.
experiments.question: When we bend things and let go, which ones spring back, which stay bent and which break?
experiments.predict: Look at the six things. Which will spring back? Which will stay bent? Which will break? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We bend each thing gently, in the middle, and hold it for a count of five. Then we let go and look. We try each thing two times, because one try can go wrong by chance.

materials.item: a plastic ruler (a 15 cm one is best)
one stick from a coconut-leaf broom, or a stiff stick from a grass broom
a strip of kitchen foil, about as long as your hand, folded into a thin flat strip
a paper clip
a rubber eraser
a toothpick, or a used matchstick
a pencil and paper for the results table

experiments.safety: Bend the ruler and the broom stick only a little, so they do not snap. A snapped toothpick has sharp ends, so put the pieces straight in the bin.

schedule.what: Guess, then bend each of six things and let go. Tick what each one does. Count how many sprang back, stayed bent and broke.

experiments.record: Tick a box for each thing in the table. Then count how many sprang back, stayed bent and broke.

setup.art: Six things in a row on a table: a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a foil strip, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick.
setup.caption: 1. Put the six things in a row. Guess what each will do.

setup.art: Two hands gently bending a plastic ruler into a small curve.
setup.caption: 2. Bend each one gently. Count to five.

setup.art: The same hands letting go, with the ruler straight again and a foil strip still bent beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Let go. Did it spring back, stay bent or break?

flow.context: This is the first step of the bend test. You guess what each thing will do.
flow.do: 1. Put the six things in a row. 2. Your child writes or says a guess for each one. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: When you bend these and let go, some may spring back, some may stay bent and some may break. What will each one do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the six things. Will each one spring back, stay bent or break? Why?

ask.q: Which one will break? Why?
good: The toothpick, because it is thin and dry.
The broom stick, because it is thin.

flow.parent: Write the guesses in the table. Do not say which are right.

flow.context: In this step of the bend test, you bend each thing and let go.
flow.do: 1. Your child bends each thing gently in the middle. 2. Hold it bent while you both count to five. 3. Let go and look. 4. Tick the right box. 5. Do each one twice.
flow.say: Bend it gently. One, two, three, four, five. Let go. Did it spring back, stay bent or break?
flow.kid: Bend it gently. Count to five. Let go. What did it do? Tick a box.

ask.q: Was anything a surprise?
good: The broom stick sprang back. I thought it would break.
The foil stayed bent even after a little bend.

flow.parent: The ruler, broom stick and eraser spring back. The foil stays bent. The toothpick bends a little, then snaps. For the paper clip, first open the outside loop a little and let go. It springs back. Then open it a lot. It stays bent.

flow.context: In this step of the bend test, you count your results.
flow.do: 1. Count how many things sprang back, stayed bent and broke. 2. Your child writes the three numbers. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: How many sprang back? How many stayed bent? How many broke? Which of these changes can be undone?
flow.kid: Count the ticks. How many sprang back? Stayed bent? Broke?

ask.q: Which changes can be undone?
good: The things that sprang back undid the bend by themselves.
I can bend the foil straight again, but a broken toothpick cannot be joined.

flow.parent: Bending the foil can be undone by bending it back, though it may keep a faint line. Snapping cannot be undone.

flow.context: This is the last step of the bend test. You say what you found.
flow.do: 1. Ask your child what was different about the two bends of the paper clip, and why they think so. 2. Then read the card 'Why some things spring back and others stay bent'.
flow.say: The same paper clip sprang back once and stayed bent once. What was different? Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: The paper clip sprang back once, and stayed bent once. What was different?

ask.q: Why did the paper clip stay bent the second time?
good: I bent it much further.
A big bend changes it more than a small bend.

flow.parent: A strong answer says the size of the bend mattered. Only after your child has said this, explain the tiny particles sliding into new places.

activities.title: Crumple and Flatten: can paper go back?
activities.context: In this activity you crumple a sheet of paper into a ball, then open it out and press it flat. You look closely to see if it is the same as before.

materials.item: two sheets of paper of the same kind, such as old notebook pages

schedule.what: Crumple one sheet. Flatten it again. Compare it with a sheet you did not crumple.

activities.record: Draw the flattened sheet. Draw the lines you can see on it.

setup.art: Two hands crumpling a sheet of notebook paper into a tight ball.
setup.caption: 1. Crumple one sheet into a tight ball.

setup.art: A flattened sheet covered in crease lines next to a smooth, uncrumpled sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Open it and press it flat. Put it next to the other sheet.

flow.do: 1. Give your child one sheet of paper. 2. Ask them to crumple it into the tightest ball they can.
flow.say: Crumple this into a tight ball. Squash it as hard as you can. What has changed about the paper?
flow.kid: Crumple the paper into a tight ball. Squash it hard. What changed?

ask.q: What has changed?
good: Its shape. It is a ball now.
It is smaller.

flow.parent: Let your child notice that the shape and the size of the paper changed. Do not explain anything yet.

flow.do: 1. Your child opens the ball and presses it flat with both hands. 2. Put it beside a sheet that was not crumpled. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Now open it and make it flat again. Put it next to a sheet that was not crumpled. Is it the same as before? What do you notice?
flow.kid: Open the ball. Press it flat. Put it next to a sheet you did not crumple. Is it the same?

ask.q: Did the change get undone?
good: The shape went back, but the lines stayed.
Some of it went back and some did not.

flow.think: Can you think of a way to get the lines out?
flow.parent: The sheet is flat again, but it is covered in crease lines that do not go away. Let your child decide whether the change was undone. Both 'yes' and 'partly' are good answers if they give a reason.

activities.title: Squeeze It: sponge, bread and a ball of foil
activities.context: In this activity you squeeze three soft things in your fist: a kitchen sponge, a slice of bread and a loose ball of foil. Then you open your hand and watch what each one does.

materials.item: a kitchen sponge
a slice of bread, or a soft idli or a piece of pav
a piece of kitchen foil, loosely crumpled into a ball

schedule.what: Squeeze a sponge, a slice of bread and a foil ball. Watch which ones spring back.

activities.record: Draw each one before and after you squeezed it.

setup.art: A kitchen sponge, a slice of bread and a loose ball of foil on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Put the three soft things on a plate.

setup.art: A child's fist squeezing a slice of bread into a small hard lump.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze each one in your fist. Open your hand and look.

flow.do: 1. Put the three things on a plate. 2. Ask your child to guess.
flow.say: You are going to squeeze each of these as hard as you can. Which ones will spring back to their shape? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which ones will spring back after a squeeze? Why?

ask.q: Which will spring back?
good: The sponge, because it is springy.
The bread, because it is soft too.

flow.parent: Many children think the bread will spring back like the sponge.

flow.do: 1. Your child squeezes each one hard in a fist for a count of five. 2. Opens the hand. 3. Watches for a few seconds.
flow.say: Squeeze the sponge. Now open your hand. Now the bread. Now the foil. What did each one do?
flow.kid: Squeeze each one hard. Count to five. Open your hand. Watch.

ask.q: What did each one do?
good: The sponge sprang back.
The bread stayed squashed in a small lump.
The foil stayed squashed.

flow.parent: The sponge springs back almost at once. The bread and the foil stay squashed. The bread has lost the air from its holes, and its soft walls stick together.

flow.do: 1. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: The sponge and the bread both looked soft and full of holes. Why do you think only one sprang back?
flow.kid: The sponge and the bread both have holes. Why did only one spring back?

ask.q: Can we undo the squashed bread?
good: No, it stays a lump.
We could pull it apart, but it won't be a slice again.

flow.parent: Two things can look alike and still act very differently when squashed. Eat the bread, or give it to the crows at the window.

activities.title: Batter to Dosa: watch breakfast change for good
activities.context: In this activity you watch a grown-up make a dosa, an uttapam or a cheela. You see runny batter turn into a solid dosa on a hot tawa, and ask whether it can go back.

materials.item: dosa batter, or any batter your family uses (besan for cheela, or rava for uttapam)
a tawa and the stove, used only by a grown-up
a small steel katori

activities.safety: Your child watches from at least an arm's length from the hot tawa, and does not touch it.

schedule.what: Watch batter turn into a dosa. Put a spoon of batter in the fridge and compare it with the dosa.

activities.record: Draw the batter, then the dosa. Draw an arrow from the batter to the dosa. Then draw an arrow going back from the dosa to the batter, and cross it out.

setup.art: A ladle pouring white dosa batter in a circle on a hot black tawa.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up pours batter on the hot tawa.

setup.art: A golden dosa on a plate next to a small katori of runny batter.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the dosa with some raw batter.

flow.do: 1. Before cooking, put one spoon of batter in a katori. 2. Put it in the fridge. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: This batter is runny. When it goes on the hot tawa, what will happen? And will cold make this spoonful change too? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel how runny the batter is. What will the hot tawa do to it?

ask.q: What will the hot tawa do?
good: It will make it hard and crispy.
It will cook it into a dosa.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours and spreads the batter on the hot tawa. 2. Your child watches from an arm's length away. 3. Point out the bubbles, the edges going brown and the top going dry.
flow.say: Watch the edges. Watch the top. What is happening to the runny batter?
flow.kid: Watch from far back. What is the batter doing on the hot tawa?

ask.q: What changed?
good: It went from runny to solid.
It went brown and crisp at the edges.
Little holes came on the top.

flow.parent: Heat makes the batter set into a solid dosa, and the brown colour is a new material forming. It is the same with besan cheela or rava uttapam.

flow.do: 1. Take the batter out of the fridge. 2. Put it beside a cooled piece of dosa. 3. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: The cold batter is still runny batter. Can we turn this dosa back into batter? What could we try?
flow.kid: Is the cold batter still batter? Can the dosa turn back into batter?

ask.q: Can the dosa become batter again?
good: No. Even if I mash it with water, it is mashed dosa, not batter.
No, the heat changed it for good.

flow.parent: Cooling the batter changed it very little. Heating it changed it for good.

activities.title: The Home Hunt: can it go back?
activities.context: In this activity you walk around your home and look for things that have been squashed, bent, twisted, stretched, heated or cooled. For each one, you decide if the change can be undone.

materials.item: paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find six changes at home. Sort them into 'can go back' and 'cannot go back'.

activities.record: Make two columns: 'Can go back' and 'Cannot go back'. Draw each thing you find in the right column.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with two columns headed 'Can go back' and 'Cannot go back', with small drawings in each.
setup.caption: 1. Make two columns on a sheet of paper.

setup.art: A child looking into a kitchen shelf with an ice tray, a jar of ghee and a packet of papad.
setup.caption: 2. Look for changes around your home.

flow.do: 1. Draw two columns: 'Can go back' and 'Cannot go back'. 2. Give one example of each.
flow.say: Ice cubes can melt and freeze again, so they go in 'can go back'. A burnt matchstick can never be a new match again, so it goes in 'cannot go back'.
flow.kid: Make two columns. 'Can go back' and 'Cannot go back'.

flow.do: 1. Walk around the home together. 2. Look in the kitchen, on the clothes line and in the cupboard. 3. Your child draws each change in a column.
flow.say: Look around. What has been squashed, bent, twisted, heated or cooled? Can that change be undone?
flow.kid: Find six changes at home. Can each one go back? Draw it in the right column.

ask.q: What did you find?
good: Ironed clothes: they can get creased again.
A cooked papad cannot go back.
Ghee is solid in the fridge and melts when warmed.

flow.parent: Good finds: a coiled phone charger wire, a squeezed toothpaste tube, ice in the freezer, ghee or coconut oil, cooked rice, a roasted papad, popcorn, a melted and set candle, a twisted hair tie.

flow.do: 1. Look at the two columns together. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the 'cannot go back' column. How many of these were heated?
flow.kid: Look at 'cannot go back'. How many were heated?

ask.q: What do many 'cannot go back' things have in common?
good: Lots of them were cooked or burnt.
Heat made them.

flow.parent: Most changes that cannot be undone in a home come from heat, or from breaking or tearing.

games.title: Undo or Not? a card game
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or 1 player sorting alone
games.context: This is a quick card game. Each card shows a change. You decide if the change can be undone or not, and hold up the right sign.

items.f: A ball of dough squashed flat
items.b: Can go back. Roll it into a ball again.
Cannot go back. Heat made a new material.
Can go back. The ice melts into water.

items.f: Dosa batter cooked into a dosa
items.b: Cannot go back. Heat changed the batter for good.

items.f: A plastic ruler bent a little
items.b: Can go back. It springs back straight.
Cannot go back. The pieces cannot join again.

items.f: A sponge squeezed in your fist
items.b: Can go back. It springs back.

items.f: A papad roasted until it is crisp
items.b: Cannot go back. It will never be a soft raw papad again.

items.f: Ghee that went hard in the fridge
items.b: Can go back. It melts when warmed.

items.f: A raw egg boiled until it is hard
items.b: Cannot go back. Heat changed the egg for good.

items.f: A wet towel twisted to squeeze out water
items.b: Can go back. Shake it out flat.
Cannot go back. Popcorn cannot become a kernel again.

items.f: A rubber band stretched and let go
items.b: Can go back. It springs back to its length.

items.f: A clay pot fired in a hot kiln
items.b: Cannot go back. Fired clay never becomes soft clay again.
Can go back. It creases again when you wear it.
Cannot go back. The wood has turned to ash and smoke.

rules: Cut out the 16 change cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile.
Each player gets two sign cards: 'Can go back' and 'Cannot go back'.
One player turns over the top card and reads it out.
Everyone holds up one sign at the same time.
Turn the card over and read the back. Everyone who was right gets a point.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. If you are playing alone, sort the cards into two piles and then check the backs.

setup.art: A pile of small cards face down, and two children each holding two sign cards.
setup.caption: 1. Shuffle the change cards. Each player takes two signs.

setup.art: A child reading a card that says 'Dough cooked into a roti', and two children holding up 'Cannot go back'.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Hold up a sign.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards together. 2. Read the rules out loud.
flow.say: Each card is a change. If the change can be undone, hold up 'Can go back'. If it cannot, hold up 'Cannot go back'.
flow.kid: Each card is a change. Can it go back? Hold up your sign.

flow.do: 1. Take turns reading a card. 2. Everyone holds up a sign. 3. Read the back and give points.
flow.say: Maize kernels popped into popcorn. Can it go back? Hold up your sign. Why?
flow.kid: Read a card. Hold up a sign. Check the back.

ask.q: Why can't popcorn go back?
good: Heat changed the kernel for good.
It burst open and became a new shape and material.

options: Ghee that went hard in the fridge
check.why: Hard ghee melts again when it is warmed. The papad and the matchstick were changed for good by heat.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the 'Cannot go back' cards. What do most of them have in common?
flow.kid: Look at the 'Cannot go back' cards. What is the same about them?

ask.q: What do most of them have in common?
good: They were heated.
Most of them were cooked or burnt.

games.title: Be the Dough: an action game
games.players: 2 or more players, with one caller
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller reads out a change, and the players act it out with their bodies. On the word 'Cooked!', players freeze in their shape until the round ends, because a cooked change cannot be undone.

items.b: Crouch down low and flat. You can stand up again.
Bend over sideways like a ruler. You can stand straight again.
Twist your body round like a wet towel. You can untwist.
Stretch up tall like a rubber band. You can shrink back.
Go stiff and still, like frozen dough. When the caller says 'Warm hands!', go soft again.
Go soft and floppy again, like dough warming up.
Jump back to how you started.
Freeze in the shape you are in now. Cooked dough cannot go back, so stay still until the round ends.

rules: Cut out the 8 call cards. The caller shuffles them.
Players stand in a space with room to move.
The caller turns over a card and shouts the word on the front. The players act it out, as the back says.
When the caller shouts 'Cooked!', every player freezes in their shape. Nothing can undo it for that round.
A player who moves after 'Cooked!' becomes the next caller.

setup.art: Three children in a living room, one crouching flat, one stretching tall, one twisting.
setup.caption: 1. The caller shouts a change. Act it out.

setup.art: Three children frozen in funny shapes while a girl holds up a card that says 'Cooked!'.
setup.caption: 2. On 'Cooked!', freeze in your shape.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the call cards. 2. Clear a space. 3. Read the rules.
flow.say: When I call a change, act it out. Most changes can be undone. But when I say 'Cooked!', you freeze, because cooking cannot be undone.
flow.kid: Act out each change. On 'Cooked!', freeze. Cooking cannot be undone.

flow.do: 1. Call out cards one by one. 2. Mix 'Freezer!' and 'Warm hands!' between the others. 3. Call 'Cooked!' near the end.
flow.say: Squash! Stretch! Freezer! Warm hands! Twist! Cooked!
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. Act out each change.

flow.do: 1. Ask the question below.
flow.say: After 'Freezer!', you could go soft again. After 'Cooked!', you could not move. Why is that?
flow.kid: Why could you undo 'Freezer!' but not 'Cooked!'?

ask.q: Why is 'Cooked!' different?
good: Freezing can be undone by warming. Cooking cannot be undone.
Heat made the dough a new material.

projects.title: My Change Diary: three days of changes
projects.context: In this project you keep a small diary for three days. Each day, you find one change you can undo and one you cannot, and draw them.

materials.item: three sheets of paper folded into a little book, or three pages of a notebook
pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Find and draw one change you can undo, and one you cannot. Write one word for each.
Find two new changes. Try to find one that was made by cooling.
Find two new changes. Then read the whole diary aloud to someone at home.

projects.record: Each page has two boxes: 'I can undo it' and 'I cannot undo it'. Draw a change in each box and write one word under it.

setup.art: A small homemade booklet with three pages, each split into two boxes.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book with three pages.

setup.art: A page with a drawing of an ice cube in one box and a dosa in the other.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, draw one change you can undo and one you cannot.

flow.do: 1. Fold three sheets into a little book. 2. Draw two boxes on each page. 3. Your child finds and draws today's two changes.
flow.say: Today, find one change you can undo and one you cannot. Look in the kitchen first.
flow.kid: Find one change you can undo. Find one you cannot. Draw them.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds two new changes. 2. Ask for one made by cooling.
flow.say: Can you find a change made by cooling today? Can it be undone?
flow.kid: Find two new changes. Can you find one made by cooling?

ask.q: What change did cooling make?
good: Water froze into ice.
Ghee went hard.
Melted candle wax went hard.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds two more changes. 2. Then reads the whole diary aloud to someone at home.
flow.say: Read me your diary. Which page has the change you liked best? Why?
flow.kid: Find two more changes. Then read your diary to someone at home.
flow.parent: Praise the reasons more than the drawings. 'I can't undo it because the heat made it a new thing' is a strong reason.

challenges.title: The Folded Paper Bridge: how many coins can it hold?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A flat sheet of paper laid across two tumblers sags when you put a coin on it. You change its shape by bending and folding, to make it hold as many coins as you can.
challenges.problem: Make one sheet of paper hold as many coins as you can between two steel tumblers. You may only bend and fold the paper.
constraints: Use one sheet of paper the size of a notebook page.
Do not use glue or tape.
Put the tumblers about a hand's width apart.
materials: sheets of paper of the same size, such as old notebook pages
two steel tumblers of the same height
a pile of one-rupee coins, or any coins of the same kind
general: Fold the paper back and forth like a hand fan, into many narrow folds, and lay it across.
Fold the two long edges up, to make walls like a gutter.
creative: Roll the paper into a tube and lay it across.
Make narrower folds, and see if more folds hold more coins.
Fold the paper into a box shape with a flat top.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own folded bridge. Count how many coins it holds before it sags down. Then change one thing and test again. Did it hold more or fewer coins?

setup.art: A flat sheet of paper sagging between two steel tumblers, with one coin on it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a flat sheet across two tumblers. Put on one coin.

setup.art: A sheet folded like a hand fan lying across the tumblers, holding a stack of coins.
setup.caption: 2. Fold it, try again and count the coins.

flow.do: 1. Lay a flat sheet across the two tumblers. 2. Put one coin in the middle. 3. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Look, the flat paper sags with one coin. We cannot use glue or tape. How could bending or folding make it stronger?
flow.kid: The flat paper sags with one coin. How could folding make it stronger?

ask.q: How could you make it stronger?
good: Fold it lots of times.
Make it thicker by folding it.
Roll it up.

flow.do: 1. Your child folds a new sheet in their own way. 2. Lays it across. 3. Adds coins one at a time and counts until it sags. 4. Tries a second design.
flow.say: Add coins one at a time. Count them. Stop when the paper sags down.
flow.kid: Fold your paper. Lay it across. Add coins one by one. Count.
flow.parent: A sheet folded like a hand fan, with folds about as wide as a finger, usually holds many coins. Let your child find this out.

flow.do: 1. Compare the counts. 2. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: It was the same paper every time. Nothing was added. Why did folding make it stronger? Can the folding be undone?
flow.kid: It was the same paper. Why did folding help? Can you unfold it?

ask.q: Can the folding be undone?
good: I can unfold it, but the fold lines stay.
Partly. The shape goes back, the lines don't.

flow.parent: Bending and folding changed only the paper's shape. The new shape made it stiffer. This is why steel sheets for roofs are made wavy.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: turn the two ends opposite ways
items.why: These four words are ways of changing a thing's shape by pushing or pulling.

items.p: In the dough test, which piece could not become a soft ball again?
items.why: The tawa changed the dough into roti, a new material. Picking the frozen piece may mean the child did not wait for it to warm up in their hands.
items.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.

items.p: Sort these changes into 'can go back' and 'cannot go back'.
items: a dosa cooked on a tawa
items.why: Freezing, squeezing and twisting can be undone. Cooking the dosa, popping the corn and boiling the egg changed them for good.

items.p: Draw the frozen piece of dough when it came out of the freezer, and again after you held it in your warm hands.
items.a: A flat, stiff disc, perhaps with frost on it, then a soft ball or a soft bent disc.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the disc stiff and flat first, then soft again, with a label such as 'stiff' and 'soft'.
items.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.
items.art: Two empty boxes side by side, labelled 'out of the freezer' and 'after warm hands'.

items.p: When you squash dough flat, it turns into a different material.
items.why: False. Squashing changes only the shape. The flat dough is still atta dough, and you can roll it back into a ball.

items.p: Say your answer out loud, and a grown-up writes it down. Why could you not turn the cooked piece back into dough?
items.a: The heat of the tawa changed the dough into roti, a new material, so it could not go back.
items.why: A strong answer says that heat changed the dough into something new, not only its shape. Saying 'because it was hard' describes it but does not say why.
items.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.

items.p: In the bend test, 6 things were tested. 3 sprang back, 1 stayed bent and the rest broke. How many broke?
items.why: 3 and 1 make 4. 6 take away 4 is 2. So 2 things broke.
items.context: This question is about the bend test. You bent a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a foil strip, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick, and watched what each one did when you let go.

items.p: Label each picture: squash, bend, twist or stretch.
labels: a hand pressing a ball of dough flat
a wet towel being wrung out
a ruler curved between two hands
items.why: Pressing flat is squashing, pulling longer is stretching, turning the ends opposite ways is twisting and curving is bending.
items.art: Four small pictures, each with an empty label line under it.

items.p: Kavya crumples a sheet of paper and then presses it flat again. She and her friend Farhan look at it.

views.says: It is flat again, so the change is undone.
It still has lines all over it, so the change is not undone.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, for example agreeing with Farhan because the crease lines stay. It also says Kavya is right that the shape and the size have gone back.
items.why: Both are partly right. The shape went back but the creases did not. Some changes can be undone only partly.

items.p: Three of these changes can be undone. Which one cannot?
opts: A ruler bending and springing back
Ghee going hard in the fridge
items.why: The roasted papad was changed for good by heat. The ice can freeze again, the ruler springs back and the ghee melts when warmed.

items.p: Put the dough test in order.
items: Cut the dough into three equal pieces
Squash one, freeze one and cook one
Try to roll each piece into a soft ball
Say which changes could be undone
items.why: First you make three equal pieces, then you change each one, then you try to undo the changes, and last you say what you found.
items.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.

items.p: In the bend test, the same paper clip sprang back once and stayed bent once. What was different?
items.why: A small bend sprang back, a big bend stayed. How far you bend a thing can decide whether the change undoes itself.
items.context: This question is about the bend test. You bent a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a foil strip, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick, and watched what each one did when you let go.

items.p: Someone says, 'Cold changes can never be undone, because ice is so hard.' Use the dough test to say what you think.
items.a: The frozen dough was stiff, but in warm hands it went soft and rolled into a ball again. So a cold change could be undone.
items.why: A strong answer uses evidence from the test: the frozen piece went soft again when warmed. That shows a cold change being undone.
items.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.

items.p: Draw a change that cannot be undone that you have seen in your kitchen. Draw it before and after, with an arrow between.
items.a: For example, white rice grains, then soft cooked rice, or raw batter, then a dosa.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the material before and after heating, and the child can say why it cannot go back.

items.p: Every change made by heating can be undone if you cool it down again.
items.why: False. Melted ghee goes solid again when it cools, but a cooked roti or a boiled egg does not go back however cold it gets.

items.p: You squeeze a sponge and a slice of bread, then open your hand. What will most likely happen?
items.why: The sponge springs back. The bread stays squashed, because its soft walls stick together. Two soft things can act very differently.

items.p: Sort these by what made the change: heating, cooling or pushing and pulling.
items: a roti cooked on a tawa
ghee gone hard in the fridge
items.why: Cooking and popping need heat. Freezing and setting need cold. Wringing and rolling are pushes and pulls.

items.p: A potter makes a crooked pot from soft clay. Before the pot goes into the hot kiln, what can she do about it? After the kiln, what can she do?
items.a: Before the kiln, she can squash the clay into a ball and make the pot again. After the kiln, the clay has become pottery, so she cannot change its shape again.
items.why: A strong answer says that squashing soft clay can be undone, but the great heat of the kiln makes a change that cannot be undone.

items.p: Draw an arrow between each pair. Write 'goes back' or 'does not go back' on each arrow.
labels: a flat sponge and a squeezed sponge
a: dough to roti: does not go back
batter to dosa: does not go back
items.why: Freezing and squeezing a sponge can be undone. Cooking dough and batter cannot.
items.art: Four pairs of small pictures with a gap between each pair for an arrow.

items.p: Priya and her Ajji, her grandmother, look at a boiled egg.

views.says: A boiled egg can never be uncooked. Nobody can do it.
I read that scientists undid a little of a boiled egg white, in a machine.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right.

opts: A change that can be undone
A change that can never be undone
A change that only happens in the fridge
quiz.why: A reversible change can be undone, like ice melting and freezing again. Picking 'can never be undone' mixes it up with an irreversible change.

quiz.p: Which of these is an irreversible change?
opts: Cooking dosa batter into a dosa
quiz.why: A cooked dosa can never be batter again. The ruler springs back and the ice melts.

quiz.p: You squash a ball of dough flat. What is it made of now?
opts: Atta dough, the same as before
quiz.why: Squashing changes only the shape. It is still the same dough. Picking 'roti' mixes up squashing with cooking.

quiz.p: Dough comes out of the freezer stiff and cold. What happens when you hold it in your warm hands for a few minutes?
quiz.why: Warming undoes the freezing. The dough goes soft again and can be rolled into a ball.

quiz.p: You bend a strip of foil and let go. What will it most likely do?
quiz.why: Foil stays bent, even after a small bend. A plastic ruler springs back. A toothpick snaps.

quiz.p: Which one is most likely to snap if you bend it a lot?
quiz.why: A dry toothpick bends only a little, then snaps. The eraser and sponge spring back.

quiz.p: Ghee goes hard in the fridge. Can this change be undone?
opts: Yes, it melts when it is warmed
No, it stays hard for ever
quiz.why: Cooling made the ghee solid, and warming melts it again. This is a reversible change.

quiz.p: In a kitchen, what makes most of the changes that cannot be undone?
quiz.why: Heating makes roti, dosa, popcorn and boiled eggs, which never go back. Squashing and cooling can usually be undone.

quiz.p: You snap a dry twig in two. Which kind of change is this?
opts: Reversible, because it is still wood
Irreversible, because the pieces cannot be joined back
quiz.why: The wood is still wood, but the twig cannot be made one piece again. Breaking is an irreversible change.

quiz.p: Before the dough test, what should you do first?
opts: Guess what will happen, and say why
quiz.why: Scientists guess first and give a reason. Then the test shows if the guess was right.

quiz.p: A potter's clay pot has dried hard in the sun, but has not been in the kiln. A piece falls in water. What happens?
opts: It goes soft and becomes clay again
quiz.why: Drying can be undone. Water goes back into the clay and makes it soft. Only the great heat of a kiln changes clay for good.

applications: Potters shape soft clay, squash it and shape it again until it is right. Then they fire it in a kiln, which changes it for good.
Cooks change food for ever with heat: rice, dosa, idli, roti and boiled eggs never go back.
Freezers keep food cold and stiff. Warming undoes the cold, so frozen peas and fish can be cooked later.
Roofs and steel sheets are made wavy, because bending a sheet into folds makes it much stiffer, like the folded paper bridge.
Springs in pens, mattresses and weighing scales use materials that spring back after they are squashed or stretched.
Ironing uses heat to press creases out of cotton. The creases come back when the cloth is worn and washed. Ruth Benerito, an American chemist, worked out ways to treat cotton so it creases less.
Glass bottles can be melted down and made into new bottles, because glass can be melted and set hard again many times.

open_questions.q: Why do most changes in the world only go one way?
open_questions.why_open: The rules for tiny particles work the same forwards and backwards. Yet a roti never becomes dough, and a broken cup never jumps back together. Physicists explain much of this, but why time itself has one direction is still argued about.

open_questions.q: Can every irreversible change be undone, with the right tools?
open_questions.why_open: In 2015, scientists undid a small part of the change in boiled egg white. Nobody knows how many other 'for ever' changes might be partly undone one day.

open_questions.q: Exactly what happens inside a bent paper clip that makes it stay bent?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the tiny particles slide into new places along lines of weakness. But predicting exactly when a metal will spring back, stay bent or crack is still hard, and engineers still study it.

maths.problem: In the bend test, a tally shows what happened: 4 things sprang back, 1 stayed bent and 1 broke. How many things were tested?
maths.explain: 4 and 1 make 5. 5 and 1 make 6. So 6 things were tested. More than half of them sprang back.
maths.context: This question is about the bend test. You bent a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a foil strip, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick, and watched what each one did when you let go.
maths.why_maths: A tally helps you see at a glance which result happened most.

maths.problem: A ball of dough is cut into 4 equal pieces. 1 piece is cooked into a roti. What part of the dough can still be rolled into a ball?
maths.explain: The dough was in 4 equal pieces, called quarters. 1 quarter was cooked and cannot go back. The other 3 quarters are still dough, so 3 quarters can still be rolled.
maths.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.
maths.why_maths: Fair tests need equal pieces, and fractions tell us how much of the dough each change used.

maths.problem: A piece of dough went into the freezer at 4 o'clock. It came out 15 minutes later. What time was it then?
maths.explain: 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour. So 15 minutes after 4 o'clock is quarter past 4, or 4:15.
maths.context: This question is about the dough test. You squashed one piece of atta dough, put one in the freezer and a grown-up cooked one on a hot tawa. Then you tried to make each one a soft ball again.
maths.why_maths: Knowing the time means every piece gets the same time in the freezer, which keeps the test fair.

maths.problem: A sheet of paper folded like a hand fan held 12 coins. A flat sheet held 1 coin, and a sheet rolled into a tube held 5. Put the three in order from strongest to weakest. What do you notice?
maths.explain: 12 is more than 5, and 5 is more than 1. The same paper held 12 times as many coins when it was fan-folded as when it was flat. Only the shape changed.
maths.why_maths: Putting numbers in order shows which shape works best, and how big the difference is.

roots.context: In the Dough Test we squashed, froze and cooked dough. In the Bend Test we bent things to see which spring back. Now we ask what changes that can and cannot be undone tell us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Dough Test, you squashed the dough, rolled it into a snake and rolled it back into a ball. Nobody looking at the ball could tell what you had done. But anyone can see that the cooked piece was heated. A change we cannot undo leaves a sign, and that sign is how we can tell what happened before.
deep_truth.habit: We think that when a thing looks the same as before, nothing happened to it. But in the Dough Test, the dough ball had been a disc and a snake, and kept no sign of those shapes. Changes that cannot be undone are the ones that leave a sign.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dough test, the squashed piece and the frozen piece both became soft balls again, and looked like the dough before. The cooked piece stayed stiff and brown-spotted, and would not become dough even in water.

three.who_am_i: You grew from a baby, and you will never be that small again. Your body carries the signs of every year you have grown.
three.what_is_life: A plant that has sprouted from a seed can never go back inside the seed. Living things grow in one direction, and their bodies show how they have grown.
three.what_is_this_world: Rocks, riverbeds and old pots all keep marks of what happened to them. Scientists read those marks to find out about the past.

roots.thread: In the Dough Test, the dough was one material that could take many shapes, a disc, a snake and a ball, and still be dough. Heat made something new from it, and the roti now carries a sign of the tawa. In the same way, the world is always taking new shapes, and some of them stay. Everything is conscious, which means aware, the dough and the clay too, and each one is changed by what happens to it. Some scientists disagree, and say only living things with brains can be aware.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka, a teacher in ancient India, told his son that by knowing one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. The pot and the plate are only names for different shapes. The clay is what is real.
teachings.link: In the Dough Test, your dough became a disc, a snake and a ball, and stayed dough all along, just as Uddalaka said of clay. The tawa showed something the teaching does not talk about: heat can turn the dough into something new.

teachings.source: Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, translated by Edward FitzGerald, first edition, 1859, verse 51
teachings.teaching: Omar Khayyam, a poet and mathematician from Persia, wrote that once a moving finger has written something, it moves on. Nothing you do can call it back to rub out even half a line.
teachings.link: Some of what happens can be undone, like a squash or a freeze. Some, like cooking or snapping, stays written for ever.

science.text: Most changes in the world happen easily in one direction and almost never in reverse. Physicists explain this with a rule called the second law of thermodynamics.
Why time seems to go only one way, from the past to the future, is still argued about by physicists.

other_view.view: They say a roti does not keep a record of anything by itself. A sign only means something when a person or another animal reads the sign. They also say dough and clay have no awareness at all.

playtest: Thought through as a parent and child in a flat. The dough test needs only atta, water, a freezer and a tawa, which nearly every Indian kitchen has. A coin-thin disc of dough goes stiff in a home freezer within about 15 minutes, and goes soft again in warm hands within about 3 to 5 minutes. A note covers using the fridge instead. A small disc cooked on a medium tawa for a minute on each side becomes a stiff roti with brown spots. Once cool, it tears rather than rolling into a ball, and in water it goes soggy but never sticky like dough. The bend test uses a plastic ruler, a broom stick, a foil strip, a paper clip, an eraser and a toothpick, all common at home. A paper clip springs back from a small bend and stays bent after a big one. Only the grown-up uses the stove.

quiz: Squashing a ball of dough changes its shape but not what it is made of.
Squashing only pushes the dough into a new shape. It is still the same dough.
A roti cooked on a hot tawa can be rolled back into a ball of dough.
Heat made a new material. A roti can never be dough again.
A rubber band springs back after a small stretch.
Its tiny particles are pushed a little out of place, and then they pull back.
If a ruler stays bent, it has turned into a new material.
It stays bent because its particles slid to new places. The material is still the same.
Chocolate that melts in the sun can go firm again when it is cooled.
The chocolate melts when it is warmed and goes firm when it is cooled, so this change can be undone.
A crumpled paper pressed flat is exactly as it was before.
The creases stay on the paper. The change is only partly undone.
Heating can turn a material into a new one that cannot go back.
Cooking dough into a roti is one example. The roti can never be dough again.
Plastic can be melted and made into new things again and again without getting weaker.
Each time, the long chain-like particles break a little. After a few times the plastic is too weak.
A ruler always springs back, however far you bend it.
Bend it too far and its particles slide to new places, so it stays bent or breaks.
A child grows taller each year and never grows shorter again.
Growing taller is a change that cannot be undone.
odd: In the first three, heating makes a new material that cannot go back. Butter can set again.
The first three only change the shape of the same material. Burning makes new materials.
The first three spring back to their old shape when you let go. Wet clay stays squashed.
The first three are breaks that cannot be undone. A rubber band goes back to its old shape.
The first three go firm when they get cold, and can melt again. Cooking an egg is heating that cannot be undone.
